examples.subject: Calendar Update: Q4 Strategy Meeting Location Change
examples.body: Good morning, please note that the location for next week's Q4 Strategy Session has moved to the Conference Room B on the 4th floor due to AV maintenance. To ensure the correct attendees are notified and the room is reserved in your personal calendar, please approve the updated invitation via the secure link below. This step also syncs the meeting agenda and pre-read documents to your shared drive folder. Please confirm your attendance by clicking 'Approve' to finalize the logistics with the facilities team. examples.subject: Routine Migration to Workday Time Tracking Portal V2
examples.body:
Hello everyone,

This is a standard notification from the HR Systems Integration team regarding the ongoing migration of our timecard and project tracking software. We are transitioning our active timesheet logs to the updated Workday Time Tracking Portal V2 over the coming weeks.

To ensure that your accrued vacation hours and current project billing codes transfer smoothly, we require all staff to validate their timesheet mappings in the new environment. The customer support and marketing divisions successfully mapped their profiles last Friday, so we are continuing the rollout to the rest of the staff today.

Please take a moment to review your projected timecard structure for the upcoming pay period and confirm that your standard project codes are accurately reflected. Doing this early helps us prevent any administrative friction when the legacy system is officially retired next month.

You can review your profile mapping and approve the transition via the HR self-service dashboard here: https://timesheet-migration-portal.online/workday-v2

We appreciate your assistance with this standard system upgrade.

HR Performance Team

examples.subject: Sun
examples.body: Well, it looks like Sun are going ahead with their ubiquitous computing plans without Mithril. Greg Reuters Market News Sun Micro Outlines Roadmap for Managing Networks Friday September 20, 5:00 am ET By Peter Henderson SAN FRANCISCO (Reuters) - Computer maker Sun Microsystems Inc. on Thursday said it would create in a few years a network environment that will be as straightforward to handle as a single machine, a strategy it calls N1. It laid out a road map for a new layer of intelligent software and systems that will meld unwieldy networks into easy-to-use systems, a goal similar to those of most rivals making computers which manage networks. EMC Corp. announced this week software aimed at allowing users to manage storage resources as a pool. Hewlett-Packard Co has a Utility Data Center, designed for broader management. International Business Machines Corp's project eLiza is working to make computers "self-healing" when systems break. "Applications still have to run zeroes and ones on some computing engine but the whole idea behind N1 is you stop thinking about that. You don't think about what box it is running on," Sun Vice President Steve MacKay, head of the N1 program, said in an interview on the sidelines of a Sun user conference. Many industry executives see computer power eventually being sold like power or water, as a utility that can be turned on or off, in whatever volume one wants whenever needed. For that to happen computers must be tied together seamlessly, rather than cobbling them together with tenuous links, as most networks do today, experts say. There are still major barriers, though, such as communications standards for machines from different vendors to interoperate closely. Sun promised to deliver a "virtualization engine" that would let administrators look at their entire network as a pool by the end of the year. Network administrators today often have no automatic system to report what is in the network. "It'll tell you what you have and how it is laid out," promised MacKay The second stage, beginning in 2003, would allow users to identify a service, such as online banking, and allocate resources for them with a few clicks, Sun said. Finally, in 2004, Sun's software should allow networks to change uses of resources on the fly in response to changing needs, such as a bank assuring quicker online response time for priority users, the company said.
